narrative:
The model estimates a 73% chance that you will leave your job. That is a high attrition risk—roughly three in four—so the promotion is being denied because the model expects you may not be there to take on the role, not because it judged your ability.

The strongest signal was your overall experience: at 6–10 years, your profile was treated as more likely to move than the typical employee expected to stay. The second signal was your tenure in the current organization: 1–5 years in this job added to that mobility risk, suggesting the model sees relatively short current tenure as a sign you may seek the next step elsewhere. The third was that you reported other job opportunities. Only about 23% of employees predicted to stay had such opportunities, so this noticeably pushed the estimate toward leaving. All three leading factors pointed toward leaving rather than staying.

Because the denial may itself affect your decision, the organization should discuss your career path and retention support with you, including a clear promotion route and recognition or reward concerns. Your own reports of not receiving the promotion you deserved and dissatisfaction with rewards should be part of that conversation. If you want to stay, make that intention explicit and agree on concrete development steps; the prediction should be reviewed as a risk signal, not treated as fixed.
